questions.title: Section A — Question 1 (Case study: nature-based farming and ecological succession)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source material is about nature-based (regenerative) farming, ecological succession on abandoned farmland, resource partitioning, pollinators and the knock-on effects of adding large herbivores. For each term in Column 1, decide which statement from Column 2 relates to it, using: 1 — only statement 1; 2 — only statement 2; 1&2 — both; None — neither.
Term: Ecosystem. Statement 1: Refers to cows grazing on cover crops, earthworms breaking down organic matter, bees pollinating flowers, and birds preying on pests. Statement 2: Refers to grazing cows enriching the soil, plants fixing nitrogen, earthworms decomposing matter, bees pollinating crops, and predators controlling pests, all interacting with sunlight, rain and nutrient-rich soil.
Term: Biodiversity. Statement 1: The variety of species in an area, including pollinators like bees, beneficial insects like ladybugs, different wild grass species, grazing herbivores like cattle and sheep, and wild carnivores like jackals. Statement 2: The many different grazing herbivores found on an African livestock farm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Ecosystem — 2 (an ecosystem includes both the living community and its interaction with the non-living factors — sunlight, rain, soil).
Biodiversity — 1 (biodiversity is the full variety of species in an area, not just the grazing herbivores).
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: The contribution of agriculture to South Africa's GDP has declined from 23% in 1920 to 2,62% in 2023. Calculate the percentage decrease in agriculture's contribution to South Africa's GDP between 1920 and 2023. Show all your workings. Round off your answer to one decimal place.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct values identified: 1920 = 23; 2023 = 2,62 (1).
% decrease = (original − new) ÷ original × 100 = (23 − 2,62) ÷ 23 × 100 (method) (1)
= 88,6% (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE land cover category from Table 1.1 that could have resulted from poor agricultural practices.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: eroded land; fallow land / old fields. Also accept: barren; semi-natural.

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source 2 and Figure 1.2. State the type of plant succession that occurs when abandoned farmland recovers naturally.
subQuestions.memoText: Secondary succession.

subQuestions.questionText: The successional states are 'Pioneer species' and 'Climax community'; the plant groups that colonise abandoned croplands are: Closed woodland, Herbaceous plants, Small trees, Annual grasses, Shrubs. Link each successional state to its correct plant group — one line from the pioneer species and one from the climax community.
subQuestions.memoText:
Pioneer species → Annual grasses (1).
Climax community → Closed woodland (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Construct a table comparing the differences between nature-based farming practices and the natural recovery of abandoned farmland in terms of: human involvement, and the biodiversity outcomes of ecological succession. No heading is required.
subQuestions.memoText:
Table construction with correct headings (1) + one correct comparison per row (2). Example:
 | Nature-based farming | Natural recovery
Human involvement | Active / a lot of involvement | Minimal involvement
Biodiversity outcome of succession | Artificially increased to a managed level / point | Naturally increases over time

subQuestions.questionText: State the ecological term that describes the coexistence of two or more species in an ecosystem by using the same resource in different ways.
subQuestions.memoText: Resource partitioning (niche differentiation).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how plants with different rooting depths illustrate the concept you named in Question 1.4.1. Provide an example from the Source Material to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: plants with different rooting depths use the same resource (soil water / nutrients) in different ways, which reduces interspecific competition for it — e.g. deep-rooted trees or legumes draw water and nutrients from deeper soil layers while shallow-rooted grasses or cover crops use surface moisture (e.g. in the Overberg, integrating deep-rooted legumes with shallow-rooted grasses improved drought tolerance).

subQuestions.questionText:
The introduction of beehives into nature-based farms can improve crop productivity.
(a) Describe the division of labour in ONE eusocial insect colony you have studied.
(b) Briefly explain how the division of labour you described in (a) provides a survival advantage to the colony.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Three castes explained (3 marks). Bees/ants: workers perform multiple tasks (feed larvae, forage for food/nectar, defend the colony, dispose of waste, build and maintain the hive/nest); the queen lays thousands of eggs (generational turnover); drones mate with the queen (add genetic diversity). OR termites: workers forage, build tunnels and nests, care for the young and keep the colony clean; soldiers defend the colony against rivals and other insects; the king and queen produce new colonies through swarming.
(b) (1 mark): each specialised caste can devote more time and energy to its own role, and specialisation makes the colony more efficient / productive, so the colony has a greater chance of survival.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why increased pollination would boost crop productivity.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: more successful pollination (between flowers of the same species) leads to more fertilisation and so more successful seed development / fruit production — a bigger crop.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why bee colonies on nature-based farms face less food scarcity and are likely to maintain larger population sizes. Use the following ecological terms in your answer: habitat diversity, and carrying capacity.
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: nature-based farms have greater habitat diversity (a wider range of flowering species), giving a more continuous supply of nectar and pollen through the year, so the bees experience fewer periods of food scarcity; this raises the carrying capacity for the bee colony, so it can sustain a larger population even during seasonal or drought fluctuations.

subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the ecological knock-on effects of nature-based farming. On the set of axes provided, draw a simplified sketch graph depicting the response of the rodent population to the reintroduction of barn owls in Kenya (Figure 1.5 A). Draw TWO lines: one for the rodent population and one for the barn owl population. No heading is required; actual population numbers are not needed.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 A in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (4): x-axis labelled (time / years / months) (1); y-axis labelled (number of individuals / population size) (1); rodent line drawn higher than the barn owl line, with the final rodent number lower than its starting number (owls control the rodents) (1); barn owl line drawn with a final population higher than or equal to its starting population (not lower) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE observation scientists would make in a wildlife game reserve if a population of large mammalian herbivores had exceeded its carrying capacity.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: habitat degradation / overgrazing / less food available; a population crash; death rate exceeding birth rate.

subQuestions.questionText:
Explain how the carrying capacity of natural grasslands in South Africa could increase under nature-based farming practices through the addition of more large herbivores (Figure 1.5 B). Provide facts from the Source Material Booklet to support your answer.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 B in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): when managed correctly (e.g. rotational grazing), more large herbivores can increase ecosystem resources rather than deplete them, allowing a larger livestock population. Supporting facts: large herbivores add manure, contributing to nutrient cycling and raising soil nutrient status (Fig 1.5 B); rotational grazing aids seed dispersal, improving plant growth, diversity and forage availability; rotational grazing improves soil structure and water retention and promotes plant regrowth, keeping forage available year-round.

questions.title: Section A — Question 2 (Case study: West African lions in the W-Arly-Pendjari complex)

subQuestions.questionText: A population is a group of individuals of the same species, inhabiting the same location at a designated time. State how these THREE population criteria are expressed in terms of the West African lion in the source material on page vi.
subQuestions.memoText:
Same species — Panthera leo leo / the West African lion (1).
Same place — the W-Arly-Pendjari (WAP) complex / West Africa / Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger (1).
Same time — the survey year given (e.g. 2016 / 2022 / 2025 / the present) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Lions are considered to be apex predators. Why are lions classified as predators?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: lions hunt, kill and eat other animals (their prey).

subQuestions.questionText: Complete the table by filling in ONE physical feature of lions and stating how it enables a lion to hunt its prey successfully.
subQuestions.memoText: One correct feature + how it aids hunting (1 mark). Examples: muscular build → strength and bursts of speed for pursuing and tackling prey; sensitive hearing → detects prey from far away; excellent night vision → hunting at night when diurnal prey is less alert; powerful shoulders / large forepaws → grab, tackle and subdue prey; tawny coat → camouflage while stalking; long tufted tail → balance when chasing prey.

subQuestions.questionText: Lions are considered the only truly social cats. Describe TWO ways in which the pride system enhances their survival.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): lionesses hunt together, raising success rates and letting them bring down larger prey; lionesses give birth in synchrony and raise cubs communally, improving cub survival through shared protection and care; males form coalitions, better able to defend the pride and cubs from rival males and secure breeding; larger prides hold better territories with more resources, lowering mortality.

subQuestions.label: 2.2.4(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source 5 and Figures 2.6–2.9. Construct a simplified food web for the WAP complex using the following organisms: Lion, Buffalo, Kob antelope, Grass. No heading is required; do not draw the organisms.
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (4): grass placed at the bottom (producer); buffalo and kob antelope placed at the first consumer (herbivore) level, both feeding on grass; lion placed at the top, feeding on both the buffalo and the kob antelope; arrows drawn between the correct organisms and pointing in the direction of energy flow (grass → buffalo → lion; grass → kob → lion).

subQuestions.label: 2.2.4(b)
subQuestions.questionText: What is an ecological niche?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: the specific set of environmental conditions a species requires and the functional role or position it occupies in its ecosystem / community.

subQuestions.label: 2.2.4(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE prey species that became MORE nocturnal because of human disturbance.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: bushbuck / reedbuck / buffalo / duiker / aardvark.

subQuestions.label: 2.2.4(d)
subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figure 2.8 and describe how increasing pastoralist activities and livestock encroachment in the WAP complex alters the temporal activity of lions.
(Refer to Figure 2.8 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2, or 1 well explained (2 marks): the lions become more nocturnal / more active at night; they contract their temporal niche and become less active during the day (mornings and early afternoon) when human encounters are most likely, so as to reduce overlap with people; the difference between their night and day activity becomes more pronounced.

subQuestions.label: 2.2.4(e)
subQuestions.questionText:
The flow chart shows steps illustrating the effect of human disturbance on the temporal niches of West African lion prey species, in an incorrect order. Arrange the steps correctly and write only the numerical sequence.
1. Decline in certain herbivore populations
2. Increased predation (selection) on certain prey animals
3. Prey become more nocturnal (in response to humans)
4. Human disturbance
5. Instability of the West African lion population
6. Greater temporal niche overlap with lions
subQuestions.memoText:
4 → 3 → 6 → 2 → 1 → 5
(human disturbance → prey become more nocturnal → greater temporal niche overlap with lions → increased predation on those prey → decline in those herbivore populations → instability of the lion population)

subQuestions.questionText:
The W-Arly-Pendjari complex spans Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger, which can all be classified as less-developed countries. Provide TWO pieces of evidence from Figure 2.2 (population pyramids) to support this statement.
(Refer to Figure 2.2 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): high birth rates; high death rates; a high dependency ratio (large 0–15 and 65+ groups); low life expectancy; a triangular pyramid with a very wide base.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain ONE way in which the high fertility rates and economic challenges in Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger could increase human-wildlife conflict.
subQuestions.memoText: One way, well explained (2 marks): a growing population that relies heavily on subsistence farming and pastoralism needs more land, grazing and water, so people encroach into wildlife areas — increasing competition with wildlife for resources, the chance of dangerous direct encounters, disease spread between livestock and wildlife, and reliance on bushmeat and poaching.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Figure 2.9 and calculate the rate of decrease per year of West African lion numbers between 2012 and 2025 in the WAP complex. Show your workings. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. (Lion numbers: about 100 in 2012 and about 25 in 2025.)
(Refer to Figure 2.9 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: Rate of decrease = (2012 number − 2025 number) ÷ (2025 − 2012) years = (100 − 25) ÷ 13 = 75 ÷ 13 ≈ 5,77 ≈ 6 lions per year (3 marks — working + answer). Accept 5–7 lions/year.

subQuestions.questionText:
Lion population numbers in the WAP complex remain far below the ecosystem's carrying capacity. Describe ONE positive and ONE negative consequence that might result from increased lion numbers, given the human-wildlife conflict in and around this Transfrontier Park.
Positive:
Negative:
subQuestions.memoText:
Positive (1): lions would regulate herbivore numbers, preventing overgrazing and keeping habitat healthy (and less wildlife damage to pastoral land); a healthy lion population would attract more ecotourism, conservation funding and (trophy) hunting revenue, creating jobs for local communities.
Negative (1): more lions would mean more livestock predation, leading to retaliatory killings and loss of farm income; poaching or habitat loss of lion prey could push more lions to hunt livestock.

subQuestions.questionText: Can wildlife conservation and agriculture successfully coexist in poorer countries? Provide TWO biologically sound arguments to support your stance.
subQuestions.memoText: A clear decision + 1 argument briefly described + 1 argument well explained (3 marks). NO: human-wildlife conflict reduces agricultural productivity — encroachment leads to crop raiding and livestock predation, then retaliatory killings and economic losses; agricultural expansion causes habitat loss, fragmentation and poaching, weakening ecosystems and reducing yields. YES: healthy ecosystems support agriculture — conserving lions controls wild herbivore numbers and prevents overgrazing of farmland; conflict can be mitigated with predator-proof fences, buffer zones and farmer compensation, and wildlife tourism/hunting creates jobs; nature-based farming and rewilding of abandoned croplands maintain biodiversity while supporting production.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Sources A–F in the Source Material Booklet (the conservation status of African lions and gaps in data; lion population estimation techniques and their precision; individual-identification, call-in, camera-trap and 'estimate from nearby data' methods; how habitat and behaviour factors affect accuracy; and the influence of stakeholders such as quota-setters, government agencies, hunting operators, funders and researchers). Consider the statement:

"The sampling methods used to determine the size of African lion populations provide an accurate estimate of their numbers."

Using the source material and your own knowledge, discuss your opinion in an essay of 2½–3 pages. You are expected to: read the sources carefully; take a definite stand; plan your essay before writing (the plan is marked); present a debated argument using relevant information from Sources A–F plus your own Life Sciences knowledge; arrange the information to develop your argument; write in a scientifically appropriate way; and discuss at least nine different facts from the sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with the IEB essay rubric (40): Planning (6); Use of knowledge from sources (8); Use of own knowledge (4); Content relevance (2); Quality of argument supporting the decision (8); Fairness — counter-opinions integrated (4); Presentation (4); Scientific merit (4). (The source-fact table accounts for a maximum of ~10 of the 40 marks — the rest comes from planning, argument, presentation and scientific merit.)

Examples of usable facts —
DO provide an accurate estimate: direct methods are more accurate, and most lion-number data comes from direct methods (B); precision is high for call-in surveys (93%), track counts (90%), camera surveys (75%) and capture-recapture (70%) (Table 3.1); individual-identification / mark-recapture is very accurate and avoids double counts, especially given lions' pride and territorial system (C); call-in surveys are cost- and time-efficient (C); camera-trap surveys are accurate when combined with individual ID (C, Fig 3.4); estimates from nearby data are accurate when the reference sites have similar habitat and lion behaviour (C); accuracy improves when methods account for vegetation density, water distribution, terrain, season and home range (D); IUCN estimates underwent peer review and researchers now cross-validate with multiple methods (F); Cameroon (2015), Kenya's nationwide standardised capture-recapture survey, and 2024 KNP, 1990s Serengeti, 2018 WAP, 2021 Kafue and 2022 Pilanesberg estimates were the same as or close to reference values (E, F, Table 3.6).
DO NOT provide an accurate estimate: reliable data is lacking for much of the lion range (Angola, CAR, Somalia, South Sudan, Ethiopia; parts of Zambia and Tanzania), and global estimates vary two-fold (~20 000–40 000) (A); of 169 peer-reviewed articles, 97 came from just three areas (South Africa, Tanzania, Asia), and over 10% were opinion- or questionnaire-based (Fig 3.2); precision is low for distance-based (50%) and secondary-information (13%) methods (Table 3.1); mark-recapture is cost- and labour-intensive and requires human interaction; call-in survey accuracy varies with lion responses (age, habitat, prey, prior human contact), and camera-trap results depend on camera placement (C); expert-opinion and interview surveys have low accuracy, recall bias, conflicts of interest and are hard to standardise (D, Fig 3.5); very large or overlapping home ranges cause double counting, nomadic lions are underestimated, dense vegetation causes underestimates and water-focused sampling causes overestimates (D); quotas in Burkina Faso, CAR and Tanzania are not based on population estimates, funding gaps limit monitoring, and some IUCN figures are accepted without rigorous scrutiny (E, F); lions are nocturnal and avoid humans, which biases sampling in high-human-density or fragmented areas (own knowledge / Q2 case study).
